Documentation of the alien's membership in associations in the field for which
classification is sought, which require outstanding achievements of their members as
judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or fields.
8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2)
In order to satisfy the regulatory criteria at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2), the petitioner must
show that the association requires outstanding achievement as an essential condition for admission to
membership. The Petitioner did not state that the Beneficiary is a member of such associations.
Instead, counsel for the Petitioner avers that this criterion is inapplicable to the Beneficiary's
occupation because "[t]he associations involved in show jumping do not require any achievements
for membership."
First, although counsel maintains that this criterion does not readily apply to the Beneficiary's
occupation, the authors of the letters submitted, including the Petitioner, do not claim that this criterion
6

Matter ofC-H- Inc.
does not readily apply.4 Without supporting documentary evidence, the assertions of counsel will not
satisfy the Petitioner's burden of establishing that comparable evidence may be considered. The
assertions of counsel do not constitute evidence. Matter of Obaigbena, 19 I&N Dec. 533, 534 n.2
(BIA 1988); Matter of Laureano, 19 I&N Dec. 1, 3 n.2 (BIA 1983); Matter of Ramirez-Sanchez, 17
I&N Dec. 503, 506 (BIA 1980). Counsel's statements must be substantiated in the record with
independent evidence, which may include affidavits and declarations.
Assuming arguendo that the Petitioner had explained why this criterion does not readily apply to the
Beneficiary's occupation, it has not shown how the evidence submitted is "comparable" to the
objective evidence required at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2). On appeal, the Petitioner avers that
"[a]djudicators should take Judicial Notice that only the best in the world of show jumping are or
have competed at the and that by virtue of their representation of their respective countries
the Riders and Trainers are all of exceptional ability." While an athletic team is not strictly speaking
an "association," it is nonetheless true that an athlete can earn a place on a national or an Olympic
team only through rigorous competition that separates the very best from the great majority of
participants in a given sport. Therefore, an athlete's or coach's membership on an Olympic team or
a major national team such as a World Cup team may serve to meet this criterion as such teams are
limited in the number of members and have a rigorous selection process. We reiterate, however, that·
it is a petitioner's burden to demonstrate that a beneficiary meets every element of a given criterion,
including that she is a member of a team that requires outstanding achievements of its me)mbers, as
judged by recognized national or international experts.
The authors of the letters submitted do not maintain, and the remaining evidence does not otherwise
establish, that the Beneficiary was elected as a member of the 2012
showjumping team or a major national team. Rather, the Petitioner avers that the fact that the
Beneficiary was hired as a trainer by and is evidence of her extraordinary
ability. Both riders maintained that and top international show riders will only select a
trainer who is at the top of his or her field. Chairman of the
indicated that the Beneficiary's "[e]xperience as a trainer for and
is evidence in itself that she is an extraordinary ability trainer." The letters of and
do not, however, provide information regarding their employment requirements or hiring
process. As a result, their statements fall short of establishing that outstanding achievements in the
horse training field are a prerequisite for employment, or that the Beneficiary has made outstanding
achievements in her field. Based on the above, the Petitioner has not shown how the evidence
submitted is "comparable" to the objective evidence required at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2).

On appeal, counsel for the Petitioner maintains that the regulation at 8 C.F.R. · § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5)
"does not apply to the trainer in show jumping .. . because the field of show jumping does not involve
the type of originality implied in this criterion," and renews its request that comparable evidence be
considered. As noted by the Director, although counsel maintains that this criterion does not readily
apply to the Beneficiary's occupation the authors of the letters submitted, including the Petitioner, do
not claim that this criterion does not readily apply to the Beneficiary's occupation. Further, as stated
previously, an inability to meet one or some of the regulatory criteria is not evidence that the regulatory
criteria do not readily apply to a beneficiary's occupation.
In addition, the Petitioner does not state what evidence, aside from the letters, should be considered as
comparable evidence. The Petitioner does not show how the letters are "comparable" evidence; rather,
it avers that they demonstrate how the Beneficiary meets the plain language of this criterion. Upon
review, the letters do not establish that the Beneficiary meets this criterion.

More importantly, while the preceding letters of recommendation demonstrate that the Beneficiary's
work has earned the respect and admiration of those for whom she has worked in the field, and that
her work has benefited them, the letters do not provide specific examples of how those contributions
rise to a level consistent with business-related original contributions of major significance in the
field as a whole. Regardless of the field of endeavor, the plain language of the phrase "contributions of
major significance in the field" requires evidence of an impact beyond one's employer and clients or
customers. Cf Visinscaia 4 F.Supp.3d at 135-6 (upholding a finding that a ballroom dancer had not
met this criterion because she did not demon'strate her impact in the field as a whole). Without
documentation showing that the Beneficiary's work has been unusually influential, highly acclaimed
throughout her field, or has otherwise risen to the level of original contributions of major
significance, we cannot conclude that she meets this criterion. Here, the evidence which the
Petitioner submitted has not established that the Beneficiary's work has had a demonstrable impact
on the field as a whole commensurate with a contribution of major significance.
As the letters do not affirm the Beneficiary's contributions to the field of show jumper horse training
as a whole, the Petitioner has not established that the Beneficiary meets this criterion. The Petitioner
has also not demonstrated that it may rely on comparable evidence or that it has submitted evidence that
is comparable to this criterion.

Evidence that the alien has been employed in a critical or essential capacity for
organizations and establishments that have a distinguished reputation. 8 C.F.R.
§ 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(7).
The scope of the evidentiary criterion at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(7) focuses on the Beneficiary
and the relative importance of her position within the scope of the organizations that have employed
her. A critical role or essential role should be apparent from a beneficiary's impact on the
organization or the establishment's activities. The record should establish whether the role was

critical for the organization or establishment as a whole. The petitioner must also demonstrate that
the organizations or establishments have a distinguished reputation.
On appeal, counsel maintains that this criterion "may" apply to the trainer in show jumping. Counsel
avers that while the "[t]he Support letters make abundantly clear that the [B]eneficiary is critical and
essential to her employers ... it is a stretch to call ... any show jumper stable distinguished." The
Petitioner did not submit evidence that the show jumper stable of either or has
a distinguished reputation in the sport, as required by the plain language of the criterion. The Director
determined that the Petitioner did not submit evidence that satisfies the plain language requirements of
this criterion.
Although counsel urges that this criterion is not readily applicable to the Beneficiary's occupation, the
letters do not corroborate counsel's contention. Regardless, the Petitioner does not state what evidence,
aside from the letters, should be considered as comparable evidence. The Petitioner does not show how
the letters are comparable evidence; rather, it avers that they demonstrate how the Beneficiary meets the
plain language of this criterion. For the reasons discussed below, the letters do not establish that the
Beneficiary meets this criterion.
The Petitioner states that the letters demonstrate the relative importance of the Beneficiary's position
within the scope of the organizations that have employed her. The letters confirm that the
Beneficiary worked as show jumper trainer for and between 2009 and
2014. At issue is whether she performed in a critical or essential role for their organizations as a whole.

Not every member of a show jumper training staff that performs effectively for the stable meets this
regulatory criterion. The record does not contain sufficient evidence to establish that the
Beneficiary's position with those organizations was in a critical or essential capacity. For instance, the
Petitioner did not provide an organizational chart or other evidence documenting where the
Beneficiary's trainer position fell within the general hierarchy of the organizations of or
such as evidence showing how it related to other trainer positions in the organization, the
number of trainers employed, or how many ofthem trained top-level horses. As previously stated, the
record lacks documentation that demonstrates the Beneficiary's established successful history of
being the principal trainer of top-level horses. The Petitioner's evidence does not elucidate how the

Upon review, although the submitted letters speak highly of the Beneficiary's performance for the
organizations that have employed her they do not establish that she was responsible for the previous
employers' success or standing to a degree consistent with the meaning of "critical or essential
capacity.'?- General statements about the Beneficiary's work being "material" or "critical" without
any description of specific instances in which she performed in an essential or critical capacity for a
particular organization are not sufficient to establish· that the Beneficiary was responsible for the
previous employers' success or standing to a degree consistent with the meaning of "critical or
essential capacity." We agree with the Director's.determination that the Petitioner has not submitted
evidence that satisfies the plain language requirements of this criterion.
